nameStory: This little bee earned its "confusing" name because it's genuinely hard to tell apart from its close relatives - even bee experts sometimes scratch their heads! The "furrow" part comes from the distinctive grooves or furrows that run across the bee's abdomen, like tiny plowed fields on its back.
description: The Confusing Furrow Bee is a small, metallic sweat bee that's about the size of your pinky nail. These bees have a bronze or greenish sheen that catches the light beautifully, with distinct grooves running across their dark abdomen. Like other sweat bees, they're attracted to human perspiration for its salt content, though they're gentle and rarely sting. They're social bees that live in small underground colonies with a queen and workers.

idTips.label: Metallic bronze sheen
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive metallic bronze or greenish glint on the head and thorax that shifts as the bee moves in sunlight

idTips.label: Abdominal furrows
idTips.description: The dark abdomen has clear horizontal grooves or furrows running across each segment, like ridged lines

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: About 8-10mm long, roughly the width of your pinky nail, smaller than a honeybee

idTips.label: Salt-seeking behavior
idTips.description: May land gently on sweaty skin to drink salt, feeling like a tiny tickle with no aggressive buzzing

idTips.label: Ground nesting
idTips.description: Look for small holes in bare soil with tiny dirt mounds nearby, often several close together

habitat: You'll find Confusing Furrow Bees in open, sunny areas with bare or sparsely vegetated soil for nesting - think garden edges, path margins, baseball fields, and sunny clearings. They prefer well-drained soil where they can dig their underground tunnels, often in areas with mixed wildflowers and weedy plants nearby for foraging.

seasonality.spring: Queens emerge from winter hideouts and begin establishing new colonies in the soil. Look for single bees investigating bare ground and early flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with workers busily visiting flowers and tending underground nests. This is the best time to spot their metallic shine and observe their gentle salt-seeking behavior.
seasonality.fall: New queens and males emerge for mating flights. Activity slows as workers die off and only mated queens prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Mated queens hibernate underground or in protected crevices. No visible activity above ground during cold months.

funFact: These bees are living mood rings - their social structure actually changes with the seasons! Early in the year they live alone like solitary bees, but as summer progresses, they form temporary societies with queens and workers, making them one of the few bees that switch between solitary and social lifestyles in a single year.
confusionNotes: All furrow bees look remarkably similar - hence the "confusing" name! The key memory trick: if you see a small, metallic bee with obvious furrows on a dark abdomen near bare soil, you're probably looking at a furrow bee, but pinpointing the exact species often requires expert examination of tiny details.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while "confusing" refers to identification challenges, these bees are actually quite predictable in their habits and easy to observe once you know what to look for. The "sweat bee" nickname sometimes makes people nervous, but they're incredibly gentle and their interest in salt is purely nutritional.
compareHints: Compared to the Ligated Furrow Bee, the Confusing Furrow Bee tends to have a more bronze (less greenish) metallic sheen. The Orange-legged Furrow Bee has distinctly orange or reddish legs, while the Confusing Furrow Bee's legs are typically dark. The Parallel-striped Sweat Bee has more obvious light stripes on its abdomen rather than just furrows.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Ligated Furrow Bee can be distinguished from its close relatives by its consistent dark metallic coloration and widespread abundance — it's the most commonly observed furrow bee in New England with over 6,000 recorded sightings.
Among the furrow bees, orange-legged furrow bees are distinguished by their bright orange legs, while ligated furrow bees have pale legs and more pronounced white abdominal bands.
Unlike the Ligated Furrow Bee which has more irregular banding, the Parallel-striped Sweat Bee has distinctly even, parallel stripes.
